power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 172 columns across 14 data files.
#### Issues Identified
4 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("ThaiPop.csv", "ThaiPop.csv", "Thai_death_age.csv", "Thai_death_age.csv"), Column = c("Age", "AgeEnd", "Age", "AgeEnd" ), Issues = c("#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 99% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"100+\"", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 99% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"null\"", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 99% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"100+\"", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 99% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"null\"" )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 14 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **8 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Files not run on their own
2 files only define functions, so running them on their own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.

"benchmark/plots/summarise.R, sim_borchering.R, data_processing.R, sim_long.R"

#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 25 scripts: 11 ran without error, 7 errored, 0 timed out, 4 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 3 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **A script looked for 5 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running it once more we copied them there: `cocirculation/plots/figS2.R` to `cocirculation/plots/cocirculation/plots/figS2.R` for `run_all.R`; `cocirculation/plots/plot_style.R` to `cocirculation/plots/cocirculation/plots/plot_style.R` for `run_all.R`; `cocirculation/summary_data/population.rds` to `cocirculation/plots/cocirculation/summary_data/population.rds` for `run_all.R`; `data/wpp2024_thai_age_windows.csv` to `cocirculation/plots/data/wpp2024_thai_age_windows.csv` for `run_all.R`; `cocirculation/plots/fig2_figS4.R` to `cocirculation/plots/cocirculation/plots/fig2_figS4.R` for `run_all.R`. **Undefined-variable errors**
**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

text.text: Dengue virus (DENV) is endemic across Southeast Asia (SEA), where a large proportion of adults have been infected.
Zika virus (ZIKV) has circulated in the region for decades but the extent of transmission remains unclear.
Prior infection with one virus can protect against or enhance infection with the other, but the population-level consequences are unknown.

We developed an age-structured DENV-ZIKV model with nine cross-reactivity assumptions combining cross-protection and subsequent enhancement, and simulated sustained cocirculation under changing Thai demography.
Through cross-reactivity, DENV strongly shaped ZIKV transmission, whereas ZIKV had little effect on DENV transmission.
Under cross-protection, ZIKV transmission occurred as infrequent outbreaks without changes in longterm ZIKV burden.
When prior DENV infection enhanced both ZIKV infection and symptomatic risk, this burden roughly doubled.
Population ageing raised the mean age of DENV and ZIKV cases by over 20 years, more than cross-reactivity did.
Simulated ZIKV case ages were closer to those reported in Thailand in 2019-2023 under enhancement of ZIKV infection and symptoms.
Over half of individuals aged 15-49 years remained ZIKV-naive under all assumptions, leaving many pregnancies at risk of congenital Zika syndrome.
Interpreting ZIKV case counts in SEA requires joint consideration of cross-reactivity, demographic change and case detection.
Dengue virus (DENV) and Zika virus (ZIKV) are closely related mosquito-borne flaviviruses transmitted primarily by Aedes mosquitoes [1, 2].
text.formatted: Dengue virus (DENV) and Zika virus (ZIKV) are closely related mosquito-borne flaviviruses transmitted primarily by Aedes mosquitoes <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: Dengue has expanded geographically and increased in incidence over recent decades, with hundreds of millions of estimated infections each year [1, 3].
text.formatted: Dengue has expanded geographically and increased in incidence over recent decades, with hundreds of millions of estimated infections each year <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3]</ref>.

text.text: DENV infection may be asymptomatic or present as an acute febrile illness [1].
text.formatted: DENV infection may be asymptomatic or present as an acute febrile illness <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: ZIKV infection is also frequently asymptomatic or clinically mild.
Its severe outcomes depend on age at infection, with Guillain-Barré syndrome in adults and congenital Zika syndrome, including microcephaly, after infection during pregnancy [4, 5].
text.formatted: Its severe outcomes depend on age at infection, with Guillain-Barré syndrome in adults and congenital Zika syndrome, including microcephaly, after infection during pregnancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>.

text.text: Large outbreaks in the Americas in 2015-2016 drew wider attention to these consequences [2].
text.formatted: Large outbreaks in the Americas in 2015-2016 drew wider attention to these consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Cross-reactivity is well established among DENV serotypes but remains unresolved between DENV and ZIKV.
Infection with one DENV serotype generates long-lasting homotypic immunity [6].
text.formatted: Infection with one DENV serotype generates long-lasting homotypic immunity <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Heterotypic immunity involves temporary cross-protection against the other serotypes, followed by antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), which can increase the risk of subsequent infection or severe disease [6, 7].
text.formatted: Heterotypic immunity involves temporary cross-protection against the other serotypes, followed by antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), which can increase the risk of subsequent infection or severe disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>.

text.text: Shared conserved antigenic features in the envelope protein of DENV and ZIKV allow cross-reactive antibodies from DENV-exposed individuals to bind or neutralize ZIKV, or to enhance infection at sub-neutralizing concentrations in vitro [8, 9].
text.formatted: Shared conserved antigenic features in the envelope protein of DENV and ZIKV allow cross-reactive antibodies from DENV-exposed individuals to bind or neutralize ZIKV, or to enhance infection at sub-neutralizing concentrations in vitro <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: Animal studies provided inconsistent evidence of DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity.
In mice, pre-existing anti-DENV antibodies increased ZIKV infection and ZIKV-associated pregnancy damage [10, 11].
text.formatted: In mice, pre-existing anti-DENV antibodies increased ZIKV infection and ZIKV-associated pregnancy damage <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref>.

text.text: However, some macaque studies found no clear effect of pre-existing DENV immunity on ZIKV infection or disease severity [12, 13].
text.formatted: However, some macaque studies found no clear effect of pre-existing DENV immunity on ZIKV infection or disease severity <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: In the other direction, prior ZIKV exposure was found to increase DENV viraemia or disease severity in mice and macaques [14, 15].
text.formatted: In the other direction, prior ZIKV exposure was found to increase DENV viraemia or disease severity in mice and macaques <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>.

text.text: Evidence in humans supporting DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity exists but is mostly from Latin America during the 2015-2016 ZIKV outbreak.
Individual-level cohort and community studies in Nicaragua used antibody measurements to determine each person's history of DENV and ZIKV infection.
High anti-DENV antibody titres were associated with protection against ZIKV infection and symptomatic disease [16, 17].
text.formatted: High anti-DENV antibody titres were associated with protection against ZIKV infection and symptomatic disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17]</ref>.

text.text: Results from a paediatric cohort showed that prior ZIKV infection increased the subsequent risk of severe dengue hospitalization [18].
text.formatted: Results from a paediatric cohort showed that prior ZIKV infection increased the subsequent risk of severe dengue hospitalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Population-level modelling work in Brazil and Colombia suggested that temporary crossprotection induced by prior ZIKV exposure can explain the unusually low dengue incidence after ZIKV emergence [19, 20].
text.formatted: Population-level modelling work in Brazil and Colombia suggested that temporary crossprotection induced by prior ZIKV exposure can explain the unusually low dengue incidence after ZIKV emergence <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20]</ref>.

text.text: In Brazil, dengue cases also became younger after the ZIKV epidemic, particularly where ZIKV attack rates were higher [21].
text.formatted: In Brazil, dengue cases also became younger after the ZIKV epidemic, particularly where ZIKV attack rates were higher <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity can affect epidemic timing, case numbers and the age of cases.
In contrast, the magnitude of ZIKV outbreaks in Southeast Asia (SEA) was far more limited than in the Americas.
In 2016, an outbreak in Singapore involved 455 confirmed cases, and dedicated surveillance in southern Vietnam identified 214 ZIKV-positive cases [22, 23].
text.formatted: In 2016, an outbreak in Singapore involved 455 confirmed cases, and dedicated surveillance in southern Vietnam identified 214 ZIKV-positive cases <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23]</ref>.

text.text: The limited reports in SEA could reflect reduced clinical expression in a DENV-immune population, limited transmission of ZIKV, or incomplete detection [24] [25] [26].
text.formatted: The limited reports in SEA could reflect reduced clinical expression in a DENV-immune population, limited transmission of ZIKV, or incomplete detection <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: DENV is endemic in many SEA countries, and most adults have been infected at least once [27].
text.formatted: DENV is endemic in many SEA countries, and most adults have been infected at least once <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: As populations across the region age, DENV immunity is retained by a growing share of older adults [28, 29].
text.formatted: As populations across the region age, DENV immunity is retained by a growing share of older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29]</ref>.

text.text: ZIKV has been documented sporadically in the region for decades [24].
text.formatted: ZIKV has been documented sporadically in the region for decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: In Thailand, routine surveillance has reported ZIKV cases consistently in recent years, including 818 cases in 2023 [30].
text.formatted: In Thailand, routine surveillance has reported ZIKV cases consistently in recent years, including 818 cases in 2023 <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Phylogenetic evidence indicates that ZIKV has circulated there over the long term [31].
text.formatted: Phylogenetic evidence indicates that ZIKV has circulated there over the long term <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Serological surveys in asymptomatic populations suggest that ZIKV exposure is more common than reported cases indicate [32].
text.formatted: Serological surveys in asymptomatic populations suggest that ZIKV exposure is more common than reported cases indicate <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>.

text.text: These surveys are difficult to interpret, as antibodies from prior DENV infection can cross-react with ZIKV in serological assays, particularly after repeated DENV exposure [8, 25].
text.formatted: These surveys are difficult to interpret, as antibodies from prior DENV infection can cross-react with ZIKV in serological assays, particularly after repeated DENV exposure <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref>.

text.text: The combined effects of DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity and population ageing on transmission have not been examined in a DENV-endemic SEA setting.

To investigate how DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity and demographic change shape transmission in SEA, we developed an age-structured model framework that tracks infection histories across four DENV serotypes and ZIKV, basing our simulations on DENV epidemiology and demography in Thailand.
We simulated sustained DENV-ZIKV co-circulation consistent with evidence of long-term ZIKV circulation [31].
text.formatted: We simulated sustained DENV-ZIKV co-circulation consistent with evidence of long-term ZIKV circulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: We explored how different combinations of cross-protection and enhancement shape the transmission, age distribution and accumulation of immunity for both viruses under ageing demography.

Comparing simulated ZIKV case ages with those reported in Thailand, we examined the extent to which observed age patterns could distinguish between cross-reactivity assumptions, and what reported cases indicate about ZIKV transmission in the region.
Finally, we discuss possible explanations for the contrast between the limited ZIKV activity reported in SEA and the large epidemics in the Americas.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: The model tracks infection and immunity to each DENV serotype and to ZIKV by age.
DENV infection with one serotype generates lifelong homotypic immunity and temporary heterotypic cross-protection against the other serotypes [6].
text.formatted: DENV infection with one serotype generates lifelong homotypic immunity and temporary heterotypic cross-protection against the other serotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Once this temporary protection wanes, the risk of subsequent heterotypic infection and symptomatic illness is modified by enhancement depending on the assumption [7].
text.formatted: Once this temporary protection wanes, the risk of subsequent heterotypic infection and symptomatic illness is modified by enhancement depending on the assumption <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Individuals are assumed completely immune to DENV after infections with two distinct serotypes.
ZIKV is modelled as a virus distinct from DENV, not as a fifth DENV serotype.
ZIKV infection generates lifelong immunity to ZIKV.
Each individual can therefore have up to three infections, two with distinct DENV serotypes and one with ZIKV, in any order.
Complete immunity to both viruses requires all three infections.
Simultaneous infections with multiple DENV serotypes or with both viruses are not considered.
Sequential infection pathways are shown in Figure 1a, with transition equations provided in Supplementary material 1, section 4.
text.formatted: Sequential infection pathways are shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1a</ref>, with transition equations provided in Supplementary material 1, section 4.

text.text: Cross-protection reduces susceptibility to subsequent heterotypic or cross-virus infection during the protected period, which lasts on average one year (Table 1).
text.formatted: Cross-protection reduces susceptibility to subsequent heterotypic or cross-virus infection during the protected period, which lasts on average one year (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: DENV-ZIKV crossprotection is assumed symmetric as a modelling simplification, and no, weak (20% reduction in susceptibility), and strong (80% reduction in susceptibility) protection levels are explored (Table 1).
text.formatted: DENV-ZIKV crossprotection is assumed symmetric as a modelling simplification, and no, weak (20% reduction in susceptibility), and strong (80% reduction in susceptibility) protection levels are explored (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Enhancement increases susceptibility to subsequent heterotypic or cross-virus infection after the protection period wanes.

We consider three enhancement configurations: enhancement of secondary heterotypic DENV infection only, additional enhancement of ZIKV infection after DENV infection, and further enhancement of DENV infection after ZIKV infection (Figure 1b).
text.formatted: We consider three enhancement configurations: enhancement of secondary heterotypic DENV infection only, additional enhancement of ZIKV infection after DENV infection, and further enhancement of DENV infection after ZIKV infection (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1b</ref>).

text.text: Combining the three enhancement configurations with the three DENV-ZIKV cross-protection levels gives nine DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity assumptions, labelled A-I (Figure 1b).
text.formatted: Combining the three enhancement configurations with the three DENV-ZIKV cross-protection levels gives nine DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity assumptions, labelled A-I (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1b</ref>).

text.text: We benchmark our model against Borchering et al. under comparable settings to check whether it captures DENV dynamics and the effect of DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity on them [19].
text.formatted: We benchmark our model against Borchering et al. under comparable settings to check whether it captures DENV dynamics and the effect of DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity on them <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: The model captures the overall pattern of post-ZIKV DENV dynamics in their simulations (Figure S1).  1.
text.formatted: The model captures the overall pattern of post-ZIKV DENV dynamics in their simulations (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S1</ref>).  <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: We use annual crude birth rates and age-specific mortality rates for Thailand from the World Population Prospects series for 1950-2100 to generate a time-varying population [28].
text.formatted: We use annual crude birth rates and age-specific mortality rates for Thailand from the World Population Prospects series for 1950-2100 to generate a time-varying population <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: These comprise estimates for 1950-2023 and medium-variant projections for 2024-2100.
The population is stratified into single-year age groups (0 to 89 years and 90+).
Births enter the youngest age group as immunologically naive individuals, ignoring maternal immunity.
Transmission is represented among human hosts and vector dynamics are not modelled.
All four DENV serotypes share the same transmission settings (Table 1).
text.formatted: All four DENV serotypes share the same transmission settings (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The basic reproduction number for DENV is set to 3 to represent endemic transmission intensity in Thailand [27].
text.formatted: The basic reproduction number for DENV is set to 3 to represent endemic transmission intensity in Thailand <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: In the absence of direct estimates for most SEA settings, the basic reproduction number for ZIKV in Thailand is set to 1.5, consistent with estimates from the 2016 Singapore outbreak (1.5-2) and from land-based populations in Latin America, such as Colombia and Guatemala (1.05-1.75) [22, 33].
text.formatted: In the absence of direct estimates for most SEA settings, the basic reproduction number for ZIKV in Thailand is set to 1.5, consistent with estimates from the 2016 Singapore outbreak (1.5-2) and from land-based populations in Latin America, such as Colombia and Guatemala (1.05-1.75) <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33]</ref>.

text.text: DENV symptomatic probability differs between primary and secondary infections [34].
text.formatted: DENV symptomatic probability differs between primary and secondary infections <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>.

text.text: ZIKV symptomatic probability is specified separately for pregnant women aged 15-49 years, based on the 2016 French Guiana outbreak [35].

Under DENV-to-ZIKV enhancement (assumptions D-I), we consider two parameterizations of ξDZ.

text.text: The recurrence intervals 175 (RI) measure the frequency of elevated transmission, defined as the average time from the start 176 of one period with monthly case number above the 75th percentile of the simulated time series 177 to the start of the next.

Within each window, we summarize age-specific immune profiles for DENV (naive, monotypically immune after one prior DENV infection, or completely immune after two), for ZIKV (naive or immune) and for both viruses jointly (naive to both viruses, immune to DENV only, immune to ZIKV only, or immune to both).
From these profiles, we calculate the overall seroprevalence of each virus.
Mean ages of DENV and ZIKV cases under each cross-reactivity assumption are also calculated within each demographic structure.
Each outcome is calculated for each run and summarized as the mean and 95% quantile range across runs.
Simulated age distributions of ZIKV cases are compared with reported Thai ZIKV cases from 2019-2023 [30].
text.formatted: Simulated age distributions of ZIKV cases are compared with reported Thai ZIKV cases from 2019-2023 <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Simulated cases are pooled over the 10 years of the ageing structure, which overlaps the surveillance period and has a similar population age structure [28].
text.formatted: Simulated cases are pooled over the 10 years of the ageing structure, which overlaps the surveillance period and has a similar population age structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: Reported cases are pooled across 2019-2023, and year-specific distributions are retained to show betweenyear variation.
Simulated and reported data are expressed as relative age-group proportions across nine age groups (0-4, 5-9, 10-14, 15-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64 and ≥65 years).
Comparing age-group proportions removes the effect of any reporting fraction that is constant across ages.
The primary measure is the total variation distance (TVD), which quantifies the overall difference between two distributions on a scale from 0 (identical) to 1 (no overlap).
For each run, TVD is calculated as half the sum of absolute differences between simulated and pooled reported age-group proportions.
The root mean squared error (RMSE) of these proportions is also calculated as a secondary measure.
Cross-reactivity assumptions are compared by mean TVD and RMSE across the 100 runs.
For assumptions D-I, the comparison is made under both the enhanced and the reduced symptomatic parameterizations (section 2.2).

text.text: Over the full simulation period, DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity affected ZIKV transmission much more than DENV transmission (Figure 2, Table S1).
text.formatted: Over the full simulation period, DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity affected ZIKV transmission much more than DENV transmission (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: When there was neither crossprotection nor enhancement between DENV and ZIKV (assumption A), ZIKV transmission persisted at a low level, with an average of 131.5 cases per 100,000 population per year and a coefficient of variation (CV) of annual ZIKV cases of 0.51 (Figure 2c, Table S1).
text.formatted: When there was neither crossprotection nor enhancement between DENV and ZIKV (assumption A), ZIKV transmission persisted at a low level, with an average of 131.5 cases per 100,000 population per year and a coefficient of variation (CV) of annual ZIKV cases of 0.51 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2c</ref>, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: DENV-ZIKV cross-protection turned this low-level transmission into recurrent ZIKV outbreaks separated by periods of very low transmission (Figure 2a).
text.formatted: DENV-ZIKV cross-protection turned this low-level transmission into recurrent ZIKV outbreaks separated by periods of very low transmission (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2a</ref>).

text.text: Stronger cross-protection made ZIKV transmission fluctuate more, with the CV of annual ZIKV cases rising to 1.13 under weak cross-protection (assumption B) and 2.81 under strong cross-protection (assumption C) (Figure 2c).
text.formatted: Stronger cross-protection made ZIKV transmission fluctuate more, with the CV of annual ZIKV cases rising to 1.13 under weak cross-protection (assumption B) and 2.81 under strong cross-protection (assumption C) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2c</ref>).

text.text: ZIKV outbreaks also became less frequent but reached higher peaks, with the recurrence intervals (RI) between them lengthening from 9.9 years under weak to 16.4 years under strong cross-protection (Figure 2a,b).
text.formatted: ZIKV outbreaks also became less frequent but reached higher peaks, with the recurrence intervals (RI) between them lengthening from 9.9 years under weak to 16.4 years under strong cross-protection (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2a</ref>,<ref type="figure">b</ref>).

text.text: ZIKV cases were thus concentrated in these fewer outbreaks, and the average annual ZIKV burden stayed close to that without cross-protection, at 131.4 and 138.1 cases per 100,000 population (Table S1).
text.formatted: ZIKV cases were thus concentrated in these fewer outbreaks, and the average annual ZIKV burden stayed close to that without cross-protection, at 131.4 and 138.1 cases per 100,000 population (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: When prior DENV infection also enhanced subsequent ZIKV infection (assumptions D-F), the average annual ZIKV burden in the enhanced symptomatic parameterization roughly doubled, to 270-285 cases per 100,000 population, relative to the burden without DENV-ZIKV crossreactivity (Table S1).

text.text: Under this enhancement, individuals with prior DENV infection were more susceptible to ZIKV and, in this parameterization, more likely to develop symptoms once infected.

In the reduced symptomatic parameterization, the average annual ZIKV burden under assumptions D-F stayed close to that without DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity, at 129-137 cases per 100,000 population (Figure S3, Table S1).

text.text: In DENV-endemic Southeast Asia, both the extent of ZIKV transmission and the populationlevel effects of DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity on either virus remain uncertain.

Our framework, which models the two-way cross-reactivity between DENV and ZIKV and extends previous DENV-ZIKV models, projected that cross-reactivity mainly affected ZIKV transmission and changed DENV transmission little [19, 21].
text.formatted: Our framework, which models the two-way cross-reactivity between DENV and ZIKV and extends previous DENV-ZIKV models, projected that cross-reactivity mainly affected ZIKV transmission and changed DENV transmission little <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21]</ref>.

text.text: In our model, population ageing changed the age of DENV and ZIKV cases more than DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity did.
The age distribution of reported ZIKV cases in Thailand was more consistent with model results in which prior DENV infection enhanced ZIKV infection and raised the risk of symptoms.

In settings with high DENV transmission, four DENV serotypes circulate against a single ZIKV serotype, so DENV immunity builds up across repeated infections and reaches most of the population, whereas ZIKV immunity remains limited [27, 32].
text.formatted: In settings with high DENV transmission, four DENV serotypes circulate against a single ZIKV serotype, so DENV immunity builds up across repeated infections and reaches most of the population, whereas ZIKV immunity remains limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32]</ref>.

text.text: In our model, DENV-ZIKV cross-protection changed the timing of ZIKV transmission, turning it into infrequent outbreaks separated by long periods of very low transmission (assumptions B, C, E, F, H and I), but kept long-term ZIKV burden close to that without cross-protection (assumptions A, D and G).
Between DENV serotypes, temporary cross-protection is known to generate multiannual DENV epidemic cycles [37].
text.formatted: Between DENV serotypes, temporary cross-protection is known to generate multiannual DENV epidemic cycles <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: Our results suggest that temporary DENV-ZIKV cross-protection has a similar effect on ZIKV transmission.
A ZIKV outbreak after many years of low activity could arise from sustained circulation, as in our model, and does not by itself indicate a new introduction.
Genomic data would be needed to distinguish such recurrences from new introductions.
The long-term ZIKV burden roughly doubled only when prior DENV infection enhanced both ZIKV infection and its symptoms (assumptions D-I in the enhanced symptomatic parameterization).
However, across all assumptions, our model projected that long-term DENV burden stayed within about 3% of that without DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity (assumption A).
This suggests that the presence of ZIKV is unlikely to affect endemic dengue over the long term.
Earlier modelling linked post-ZIKV dengue declines in Brazil and Colombia to temporary cross-protection from ZIKV infection [19, 20].
text.formatted: Earlier modelling linked post-ZIKV dengue declines in Brazil and Colombia to temporary cross-protection from ZIKV infection <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20]</ref>.

text.text: Those declines followed outbreaks that infected a large share of the population within a short period, so many individuals were cross-protected against DENV at the same time [38].
text.formatted: Those declines followed outbreaks that infected a large share of the population within a short period, so many individuals were cross-protected against DENV at the same time <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref>.

text.text: In our model, under sustained co-circulation, ZIKV infections were spread over time, so fewer individuals were cross-protected against DENV at any one time.
Where ZIKV circulates continuously, as phylogenetic evidence suggests for Thailand, dengue trends may show little signal of ZIKV transmission [31].
text.formatted: Where ZIKV circulates continuously, as phylogenetic evidence suggests for Thailand, dengue trends may show little signal of ZIKV transmission <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity acts through prior immunity to the other virus, and population ageing shifted the age at which the immunity was acquired.

In Thailand, the mean age of reported dengue haemorrhagic fever cases rose from 8.1 years in 1981 to 24.3 years in 2017, and a modelling study estimated that shifts in the age structure of susceptibility explained 58% of this rise [29].
text.formatted: In Thailand, the mean age of reported dengue haemorrhagic fever cases rose from 8.1 years in 1981 to 24.3 years in 2017, and a modelling study estimated that shifts in the age structure of susceptibility explained 58% of this rise <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: In our simulations, with transmission parameters fixed, the mean age of DENV cases rose by a comparable amount, from about 9 years in the young-age structure to 22 years in the ageing structure.
A rise of this size in the age of dengue cases is possible without any decline in transmission.
Ageing shifted susceptibility to older ages and raised the age of cases for both viruses.

DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity changed only the susceptibility of individuals with a given infection history within the age structure shaped by ageing, shifting the age of DENV and ZIKV cases by up to about 7 years across assumptions A-I and both symptomatic parameterizations.
Ageing also slowed the supply of new DENV-susceptible individuals through births, so DENV transmission relied more on periodic epidemics and became more variable over time.
This is consistent with the longer intervals between dengue epidemics associated with declining birth rates in Thailand [39].
text.formatted: This is consistent with the longer intervals between dengue epidemics associated with declining birth rates in Thailand <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref>.

text.text: Ageing had a similar effect on ZIKV transmission wherever DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity produced recurrent outbreaks (assumptions B-I).
Similar changes in age patterns and temporal variability may occur elsewhere in SEA, where populations are also ageing [28].
text.formatted: Similar changes in age patterns and temporal variability may occur elsewhere in SEA, where populations are also ageing <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: Projected ZIKV seroprevalence in our model was lower than DENV seroprevalence under all cross-reactivity assumptions (about 30-50% vs over 80%; Figures S5-S10).
text.formatted: Projected ZIKV seroprevalence in our model was lower than DENV seroprevalence under all cross-reactivity assumptions (about 30-50% vs over 80%; Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">S5-S10</ref>).

text.text: The mean age of ZIKV cases stayed closer to that of the whole population than the mean age of DENV cases did (Figure 4).
text.formatted: The mean age of ZIKV cases stayed closer to that of the whole population than the mean age of DENV cases did (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>).

text.text: As the population aged, ZIKV infection moved further into adulthood, and a growing share of women reached reproductive age without prior ZIKV infection.

Even when prior DENV infection enhanced ZIKV infection (assumptions D-I), our model projected that over half of individuals aged 15-49 years remained ZIKV-naive in the ageing structure (Figures S8-S10).
text.formatted: Even when prior DENV infection enhanced ZIKV infection (assumptions D-I), our model projected that over half of individuals aged 15-49 years remained ZIKV-naive in the ageing structure (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S8-S10</ref>).

text.text: Most of these individuals had prior DENV infection (Figures 3b and S12).
text.formatted: Most of these individuals had prior DENV infection (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3b</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S12</ref>).

text.text: Under DENV-ZIKV cross-protection (assumptions B, C, E, F, H and I), these susceptible adults could accumulate during the long periods between ZIKV outbreaks.
A subsequent outbreak could then infect many women of reproductive age within a short period.
ZIKV-naive women may remain at risk of ZIKV infection during pregnancy, which can cause congenital Zika syndrome [5].
text.formatted: ZIKV-naive women may remain at risk of ZIKV infection during pregnancy, which can cause congenital Zika syndrome <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Further research is needed to determine the impact of prior dengue immunity specifically on the risk of congenital Zika syndrome.
The shift of ZIKV infection towards adults, most of whom carry DENV immunity, also matters beyond pregnancy, as ZIKV infection in adults has been linked to Guillain-Barré syndrome [4].
text.formatted: The shift of ZIKV infection towards adults, most of whom carry DENV immunity, also matters beyond pregnancy, as ZIKV infection in adults has been linked to Guillain-Barré syndrome <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: The comparison of our model results with Thai data was informative about whether prior DENV infection enhanced ZIKV infection and symptoms.
In vitro and mouse studies have shown that antibodies from prior DENV infection can enhance ZIKV infection, although studies in macaques found no such effect [9, 10, 12, 13].
text.formatted: In vitro and mouse studies have shown that antibodies from prior DENV infection can enhance ZIKV infection, although studies in macaques found no such effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: Our comparison is consistent with this mechanism that prior DENV infection can enhance subsequent ZIKV infection at the population level in DENV-endemic settings.
Reported ZIKV case ages were closer to simulations with this enhancement only when it also raised the risk of symptoms.
With the lower symptomatic risk after DENV infection, simulated ZIKV cases were younger and further from the reported ages than without enhancement.

DENV-ZIKV cross-protection and ZIKVto-DENV enhancement had little effect on the age of ZIKV cases, so the comparison could not further identify which assumptions with these mechanisms best matched the reported data.
Within ages 15-44 years, reported cases were older than simulated cases in both symptomatic parameterizations.
This may reflect a higher symptomatic risk in adults with prior DENV infection than assumed, or age-dependent detection, such as differences in health-care seeking by age.
Current surveillance data cannot distinguish between these explanations.
Estimates of how DENV immune history affects symptomatic ZIKV infection in adults, who made up most reported cases in Thailand, would help interpret ZIKV case ages in SEA.
The excess of reported cases among infants under 1 year may reflect the follow-up of ZIKV-infected pregnant women and their newborns in Thai surveillance [40, 41].
text.formatted: The excess of reported cases among infants under 1 year may reflect the follow-up of ZIKV-infected pregnant women and their newborns in Thai surveillance <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41]</ref>.

text.text: The high infant share in 2021, a year with few reported cases, is consistent with this follow-up (Table S4).
text.formatted: The high infant share in 2021, a year with few reported cases, is consistent with this follow-up (Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: The age distribution of reported ZIKV cases in Thailand may therefore partly reflect who is tested.
Surveillance of pregnant women and newborns remains essential for detecting congenital outcomes, but it cannot measure the extent of ZIKV infection in the population.
Enhancement of ZIKV infection by maternal DENV antibodies could also contribute to the infant excess.
Maternal immunity was not included in our model and could be assessed in future work.
DENV-to-ZIKV enhancement raised the proportion of the population with prior ZIKV infection from about 30% to about 50% (Figures S8-S10).
text.formatted: DENV-to-ZIKV enhancement raised the proportion of the population with prior ZIKV infection from about 30% to about 50% (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S8-S10</ref>).

text.text: These additional infections occurred mainly in individuals with prior DENV infection, and ZIKV immunity was acquired at younger ages (Figures S11-S13).
text.formatted: These additional infections occurred mainly in individuals with prior DENV infection, and ZIKV immunity was acquired at younger ages (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">S11-S13</ref>).

text.text: If prior DENV infection lowers the risk of ZIKV symptoms, most of these infections would not be detected as cases [17].
text.formatted: If prior DENV infection lowers the risk of ZIKV symptoms, most of these infections would not be detected as cases <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: In our reduced symptomatic parameterization, the long-term number of ZIKV cases stayed close to that without this enhancement (Table S1).
text.formatted: In our reduced symptomatic parameterization, the long-term number of ZIKV cases stayed close to that without this enhancement (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: ZIKV immunity could then build up earlier in life without an increase in reported cases.
This is one plausible reason why no reported ZIKV circulation in DENVendemic SEA has approached the scale of outbreaks in the Americas, where ZIKV spread through largely naive populations [38].
text.formatted: This is one plausible reason why no reported ZIKV circulation in DENVendemic SEA has approached the scale of outbreaks in the Americas, where ZIKV spread through largely naive populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref>.

text.text: In other SEA settings, as in Singapore, sporadic infections and small clusters have been detected since the 2016 outbreak, but surveillance is limited by diagnostic capacity and the misclassification of ZIKV infections as dengue [24, 42].
text.formatted: In other SEA settings, as in Singapore, sporadic infections and small clusters have been detected since the 2016 outbreak, but surveillance is limited by diagnostic capacity and the misclassification of ZIKV infections as dengue <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">42]</ref>.

text.text: Serology does not resolve this in DENV-immune populations, as antibodies from prior DENV infection cross-react with ZIKV [24, 25].
text.formatted: Serology does not resolve this in DENV-immune populations, as antibodies from prior DENV infection cross-react with ZIKV <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref>.

text.text: In our model results, the age of cases was shaped mainly by population structure, so comparisons of case age over time would require age standardization.
Recording case age in single years would help detect the smaller shifts associated with DENV-to-ZIKV enhancement.
Serological surveys that can separate ZIKV from DENV immunity would show how ZIKV immunity is distributed by age, including among women of reproductive age.
Where ZIKV has not circulated continuously, new introductions into SEA populations with high DENV immunity remain possible.
Future work could assess how DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity and population ageing shape the consequences of such introductions.
The effect of prior ZIKV infection on dengue vaccine efficacy has yet to be established and should be considered [43].
text.formatted: The effect of prior ZIKV infection on dengue vaccine efficacy has yet to be established and should be considered <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[43]</ref>.

text.text: In the phase 3 trial of the dengue vaccine TAK-003, children were enrolled in eight countries from September 2016 [44].
text.formatted: In the phase 3 trial of the dengue vaccine TAK-003, children were enrolled in eight countries from September 2016 <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[44]</ref>.

text.text: In the first year after vaccination, the placebo groups at most Latin American sites had few dengue cases, which increased in the following two years [44].
text.formatted: In the first year after vaccination, the placebo groups at most Latin American sites had few dengue cases, which increased in the following two years <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[44]</ref>.

text.text: This period followed the 2015-2016 ZIKV epidemic, after which dengue incidence in the region was unusually low [19, 20].
text.formatted: This period followed the 2015-2016 ZIKV epidemic, after which dengue incidence in the region was unusually low <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20]</ref>.

text.text: Temporary cross-protection from prior ZIKV infection may have contributed to the low case numbers, but this was not assessed in the trial.
The effect of prior ZIKV infection on dengue vaccine efficacy may differ between settings and remains to be explored.
In Thailand, where TAK-003 has been licensed, dengue vaccination would add vaccine-induced DENV immunity in a population with ongoing DENV and ZIKV transmission [45].
text.formatted: In Thailand, where TAK-003 has been licensed, dengue vaccination would add vaccine-induced DENV immunity in a population with ongoing DENV and ZIKV transmission <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[45]</ref>.

text.text: Whether vaccine-induced DENV immunity affects subsequent ZIKV infection, as infection-induced DENV immunity may do, is unknown.
Data on both viruses from dengue vaccine studies would allow future work to examine these impacts across SEA within the same framework.
This work used a deterministic framework without explicit vector dynamics.

Transmission parameters were set from previous estimates, and the strength and duration of cross-protection and enhancement were set from previous studies or varied across plausible levels to explore their population-level effects.
Our results therefore show broad patterns in these effects.
Future cohort estimates of the strength and duration of cross-protection and enhancement could be used within the same framework to quantify these effects.
Our findings provide model-based evidence on the population-level impacts of DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity in a setting with high DENV transmission.
In such a setting, DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity can change the timing and size of ZIKV transmission while having little effect on dengue.
In ageing populations, a growing share of adults may remain susceptible to ZIKV.

In Thailand and other SEA settings with high DENV immunity and ageing populations, interpreting DENV and ZIKV case counts requires joint consideration of cross-reactivity, demographic change and case detection.
